titre: Did Eddington Cheat to Confirm Einstein in 1919?
accroche: A plate judged a failure gave almost half the expected deflection. Remeasured sixty years later, it switched sides.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 29, 1919, a total solar eclipse crosses the South Atlantic. Two British expeditions take position along its path: one at Sobral, in northeastern Brazil, led by the Astronomer Royal Frank Dyson; the other on the island of Príncipe, off the coast of West Africa, where Arthur Eddington is stationed. Their instrument: to photograph, during the few minutes of darkness, the stars visible close to the eclipsed Sun, to see whether their apparent position shifts under the pull of its gravity, as Einstein's general relativity, published in 1915, predicted.

## Two Telescopes, Three Numbers

Two theoretical values bracket the experiment. Treated as an ordinary mass under Newtonian gravity, light should deflect by 0.87 arcseconds at the Sun's edge. Einstein's general relativity predicts double that: 1.75 arcseconds.

At Sobral, two telescopes photograph the eclipse. The first, a 4-inch lens, is the best focused: its plates, measured and reduced by Dyson's team, give 1.98 arcseconds. The second, an astrographic telescope fitted with a coelostat mirror, loses its focus during the session, probably because the Sun's heat warps the mirror; its reduction gives 0.93 arcseconds, almost exactly the Newtonian half-value. At Príncipe, cloudy skies let Eddington photograph only five stars on two plates; his different reduction method gives 1.61 arcseconds, with a margin of error of 0.30.

In their 1920 report, Dyson, Eddington, and Davidson discard the astrographic value and keep the other two. The published conclusion leans clearly toward Einstein.

## The Discarded Number, Remeasured Sixty Years Later

The story most often told since then, popularized by a 1980 study by philosopher of science John Earman and physicist Clark Glymour, holds that Eddington, already convinced of his friend Einstein's theory, discarded the inconvenient result so the conclusion would come out as he wished: a number close to the Newtonian half-value would have been sacrificed to his conviction.

In 1979, astronomer Geoffrey Harvey remeasures the original astrographic plates, preserved at the Royal Greenwich Observatory, with a comparator far more precise than the 1919 instruments. His result: 1.55 arcseconds, with a margin of 0.34, far from the Newtonian half-value and close to Einstein's. Combined with a new measurement of the 4-inch plates (1.90, margin 0.11), his overall estimate reaches 1.87 arcseconds, within one standard deviation of Einstein's prediction.

The 1919 plate was not inconvenient because it contradicted Einstein: it was poorly measured, and would have stayed that way until someone remeasured it. Science historian Daniel Kennefick, who reopened the Dyson-Eddington correspondence in 2007, further shows that it was Dyson, not Eddington, who first proposed discarding the astrographic data, for a technical reason recorded before any result was known.

One question the reanalysis does not close: how many other classic results owe their tidiness to an instrument that no one has yet bothered to remeasure?

repere.texte: Remeasured in 1979 with a more precise comparator, the astrographic plates discarded in 1919 give 1.55 arcseconds (margin 0.34), against 0.93 in the original reduction: far from the Newtonian half-value of 0.87 and close to Einstein's 1.75.
repere.source: Harvey, G. M., “Gravitational Deflection of Light: A Re-examination of the Observations of the Solar Eclipse of 1919,” The Observatory, 99, 195-198, 1979

carte.punch: The result tossed out in 1919 to save Einstein wasn't inconvenient: it was wrong
carte.idee: In 1919, one photographic plate gave almost half the light deflection Einstein predicted; discarded from the final result, it fed a suspicion of cheating. Remeasured in 1979 with better instruments, it gives 1.55 arcseconds, close to Einstein and far from the Newtonian value.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Kennefick, D., “Not Only Because of Theory” (arXiv:0709.0685, 2007), full text
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The details of the Dyson-Eddington correspondence, and the three successive reanalyses of the Sobral plates.

quiz.question: Why is the value discarded in 1919 no longer seen as proof that Eddington cheated?
choix: Because Eddington publicly admitted to removing it out of personal conviction
Because a 1979 remeasurement, with a more precise comparator, gives a result close to Einstein's for that same plate
Because the 4-inch Sobral telescope later gave exactly the same value as the discarded astrographic plate
Because only the Príncipe measurement was ultimately kept in the 1920 report
quiz.explication: The astrographic plate gave 0.93'' in 1919, close to the Newtonian half-value; remeasured in 1979 with a more precise instrument, it gives 1.55'' ± 0.34'', consistent with Einstein. Nothing shows that Eddington removed a correct measurement, and the 1920 report keeps two instruments, not one.
